What are we looking for? What kinds of arguments are there? And how does the kind of argument change the way we word it?
This is maybe one of the most important stages. Finding the most suitable arguments for the essay.
Notice, I said the most suitable. I didn't say the best.
First, because there's no such thing as the best argument. There's no calculator where you put in an argument and, hop, it gives you a score.
And second, when you choose arguments, there are other things to think about besides how strong they are.
For example, I might prefer an argument that's a bit less strong, but still strong enough, because it's really creative. One that'll impress the rater, because not many people thought of it.
We'll learn a few techniques for finding arguments. And it's important to master all of them, because one technique may suit one task better, and another technique, another task.
First: the task itself. It usually gives you the main argument of each side. You can use them, as long as you use them well.
Second: who is involved, and how does it affect them? Not only who wins and who loses. The same person can gain in one way, and lose in another.
Third: points of view. We make ourselves look at the issue from one direction, then another, then another. You'll be surprised how many arguments you find just by doing that.
The first way is the simplest, so we'll do it right here. The other two get their own lessons.

So, way one. The task usually states the main argument of each side. In the camera task, supporters say it would reduce crime, and opponents say it would seriously harm privacy. You can use them. They're the heart of the debate. But, there are three conditions.
One: not only them. If your whole essay is just the two arguments from the task, you haven't shown the rater any thinking of your own. Add at least one argument you found yourself.
Two: not word for word. Take the idea, not the sentence.

And three, the most important one: explain it well. The task only gives you the claim. It never explains how it happens. That's your job. And that's where the chain comes in. It gets its own lesson later.
And the other side's argument from the task? Keep it. That's usually the one you'll answer in your rebuttal paragraph.
Let's see the difference.
This one is copied, and it doesn't explain anything. The rater has already read that sentence, in the task.
This one takes the same idea, says it in my own words, and explains the steps. They know they can be identified, the chance of being caught goes up, they think twice, and the areas become safer.
Now, types of argument. What is an argument? Well, it's something I claim. It's not necessarily my opinion.
Like we saw in the critical thinking lesson, an argument can be an opinion, a reasonable assumption, or a fact. And the closer it is to a fact, the stronger it is.
And that goes for every small step in the development too. Not, I think, and I think, and I think. But: it is likely that this will cause that. Then people agree with you more easily.
One more thing: the wording of the argument.
The difference between opinion, reasonable assumption and fact also changes how you word the argument.
An opinion argument starts with: in my opinion. In my opinion, face-recognition cameras will deter offenders and reduce crime.
So here it's an opinion. That's why I wrote, in my opinion. It's not certain the cameras will deter. That's my opinion. And I also think that deterring people will reduce crime. Again, my opinion.
So that's the rule for every key sentence. It starts with, in my opinion, or, I believe that.
Now, an advanced option. The standard start, in my opinion, is always correct. But when the first part of your sentence is a fact, you can put in my view in the middle instead.
Look at this argument. The database will eventually have to be accessible to people, and in my view, even if only a few people have access, there is a risk that it will leak.
The first part is a fact. If the database just sits in some cloud and nobody ever sees the footage, it can't be used. So obviously, some people will have to see it.
So I add, in my view, only in the middle, because I started with a fact.
Why bother? Well, it keeps the fact a fact, and marks only the second part as my opinion. It's optional. If you're not sure, just start with in my opinion, like always.
So the difference between the types of argument affects the wording too.
Most suitable, not best. As many facts and reasonable assumptions as you can. And start each key sentence with, in my opinion.
